newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FDA seeks action on "morning after" pill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FDA seeks action on "morning after" pill.

text.p: U.S. health officials on Monday endorsed the so-called "morning after" pill as a safe way of avoiding pregnancy and urged the makers of certain birth control pills to formally seek approval for such use.

Birth control pills have been legal for years and are used routinely by millions of women to avoid getting pregnant. A different dosage of the pill can be used the "morning after" to prevent a pregnancy after rape or unprotected sexual intercourse.

Once a drug is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for a specific purpose, doctors have the discretion to prescribe it for other uses, which is called "off-label use." But the drug cannot be advertised or promoted for those unapproved uses.

In rape crisis centres, emergency rooms and some reproductive clinics, doctors have used the birth control pill as a morning after pill but the FDA move to formally clear it for this purpose would clear up any confusion or hesitancy about its emergency use and should make it more accessible.

The FDA in an unusual move invited the makers of certain birth control pills to submit the application required to start the approval process. A formal notice will appear in Tuesday's federal register.
The morning after pill is not the same as RU 486, the so-called French abortion pill, which can cause a miscarriage two months into a pregnancy.
The agency declined, however, to approve the drug based on a petition from women's health and advocacy groups rather than from a more traditional pharmaceutical sponsor.

Approval of a morning after pill has been controversial because some anti-abortion groups consider it a form of nonsurgical abortion. They say it could make women more lax about unprotected sex if they can then run out and get an emergency dose of this drug.
Advocates, however, say women should have the extra protection in emergencies, whether it's a sexual assault or a broken condom.
"We are thrilled by what the FDA has done," said Planned Parenthood Federation of America president Gloria Feldt.
"This may reduce the number of unintended pregnancies, and prevent abortions," she said, adding that an estimated 60 percent of U.S. pregnancies are unplanned.

The morning after pill prevents pregnancy in the first 72 hours after unprotected intercourse. The FDA found it safe and effective but has not granted U.S. approval until manufacturing and labeling questions are worked out.

A federal advisory panel last June ruled that large doses of certain birth control pills could be used safely and effectively for 72 hours after unprotected intercourse to avoid pregnancy. The FDA notice in the federal registry lays out advice about the doses and timing of treatment.
The advisory panel ruling applied to six of the few dozen brands of birth control pills, containing specific formulas of ethinyl estradiol and norgestrel or levonorgestrel.
